name: Tara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I have lectures in discrete maths and programming, usually from nine until one. Then I eat in the library cafe with two girls from my corridor, and in the afternoons there are labs where we write C code and hand it in on paper first, which I like. On Thursdays I go to the student union meeting because I want to be a course representative. I live in a flat with four others about ten minutes from campus, and my mum phones every evening at eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Before we start the pictures, what made you pick computer engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad has an electrical contracting firm, and I grew up in the van handing him cable. I liked how circuits behave the same way every time. I got top marks at school and a place at a good university, so my parents pay the fees and rent and I have no debt. I know that makes me lucky, and I try not to forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time people calmed down. I've sat through two years of teachers telling us this software would change everything, and so far it writes bad essays and wrong code. If it just saves a few minutes on boring jobs, fine, I won't miss those minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel relieved. My degree is a four-year plan and I'd like it to mean the same thing at the end as it does now. My worry would be companies still using the hype as an excuse to cut junior staff and pay less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, and keep writing my own code line by line. I'd run for course representative in the spring and push the department to keep exams on paper. I'd also keep my Saturday volunteering at the repair cafe, where we fix old radios and toasters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. A bit boring, which is how I like it. I'd still keep an eye on who gets blamed when a company says a machine did the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say you'd keep exams on paper, is that about AI or about something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. If students use these tools for coursework, the marks stop meaning much, and then the people who worked honestly lose out. I'd rather the department checks what each student can do in a room with a pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel relieved. Is anything about this picture still unsettling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my dad's firm. Even in a quiet world, quoting and scheduling software gets better, and he already complains that customers expect an answer within the hour. Small trades like his get squeezed by cheap apps even when nothing dramatic happens.

say: I'd tell friends the **hype** is overblown and we should judge tools by what they actually do.
I'd say a degree should still mean **honest work**, so exams stay on paper.
think: I feel **relieved**, because my four-year plan keeps its value.
I still worry my dad's **small firm** gets squeezed by cheap booking apps.
do: Keep writing my own **code** line by line in every lab.
Run for **course representative** in the spring and push for paper exams.
Keep volunteering Saturdays at the **repair cafe** fixing old radios.
feel: Steady and a little **bored**, which suits me fine.
S0.quote: I'd rather the department checks what each student can do in a room with a pencil.
fieldNote: Resistant to AI tools but not **alarmed**; defends the old way of doing things as a matter of fairness.
Money is no worry, so her unease is about **fair marking** and her father's firm.
Left-leaning: reaches first for the student union rather than for personal tricks.

steps.text: Keep writing every lab program by hand, without AI help
Stand for course representative and ask for paper exams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules, and fast. If software takes over writing, checking and coding, then the people who lose entry jobs need protection, not a speech about adapting. I'd say that at the union meeting and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm nervous. I picked computer engineering because there are plenty of graduate jobs, and this picture is the one where that stops. I don't use these tools at all, and I feel behind already, even though nobody has told me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my degree, push the engineering side towards hardware and embedded systems, because that part is slower to automate. I'd join the union's campaign for a rule that firms must say when software replaced a role. I'd also finally try one of the coding assistants for a week, so I can argue about it properly rather than from fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at a train platform while the timetable gets rewritten. My own job isn't gone, I haven't even got one yet, but the ones I'm aiming for might be thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try an assistant for a week. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, really. I like knowing every line is mine. And I think the first time I lean on it, I'll never write a hard function from scratch again, the way my cousin stopped doing sums after getting a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that sell this software and cut staff the same quarter get the savings, and everyone else gets the bill. Not the students, not the lecturers. I'd also blame my own government for acting as if it can wait. If I had to choose one, I'd say the firms.

say: I'd say we need **rules**, and that people losing entry jobs need protection.
I'd ask firms to **say openly** when software replaced a role.
think: I'm **nervous**, because graduate jobs are why I chose this degree.
I feel **behind** on tools I have never touched.
do: Steer towards **hardware** and embedded systems, which are slower to automate.
Join the union's campaign for a **disclosure rule** on replaced roles.
Try one coding assistant for **a week** so I can argue from experience.
feel: Like standing on a **platform** while the timetable is rewritten.
S1.quote: Companies that sell this software and cut staff the same quarter get the savings, and everyone else gets the bill.
fieldNote: **Pride** in doing her own work is what keeps her away from AI tools, and she knows it.
Blames employers and government, not students; wants collective answers.
Family money means her unease is about future jobs, not this year.

steps.text: Take the embedded systems and hardware modules next term
Back the union campaign for a rule on disclosing replaced roles
Test one coding assistant for a week and write up the results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this can't be left to markets alone. Two years is nothing. I'd want a public plan on pay, retraining and what happens to everyone whose work disappears, and I'd say so loudly online and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. I'd have just finished first year, the degree would take another three, and by the time I'd graduate the thing I trained for would already be done by software. Robots come later, so my dad's cable work lasts a bit longer, but the planning and quoting side of it goes at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay enrolled, because I have nothing better, but I'd spend my summers learning a hands-on trade skill. I'd ask my dad to teach me wiring properly and get the electrician's licence. I'd also throw myself into the union and into demanding a public plan, because I don't think my own choices would matter as much as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being told the building is on fire when you're still looking for the exit sign. I'd be angry before I was scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your family's money change how you'd handle this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can take the risk of waiting and not take a bad job tomorrow. But money doesn't tell me what to study. My parents would pay for any course I pick, and I'd still not know which one is safe, and that is a strange kind of freedom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your parents something different from what you tell me?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, because she'd worry for a week. I'd tell my dad directly that I'd like to learn his trade properly, which would make him happy and a bit sad. Here I can say I'm scared that nothing I choose is safe.

say: I'd say two years is nothing and we need a **public plan** now.
I'd push online and at the union for **pay and retraining** guarantees.
think: I'd be **frightened**, because the degree finishes after the thing I trained for is automated.
I'd see my dad's quoting and **planning** work go first.
do: Stay enrolled and spend summers learning **wiring** with my dad.
Aim for the **electrician's licence** as a safety net.
Throw myself into union work and demands for a **public plan**.
feel: **Angry** before scared, like being told the building is on fire.
Strange **freedom**, since money doesn't say which course is safe.
S2.quote: My parents would pay for any course I pick, and I'd still not know which one is safe, and that is a strange kind of freedom.
fieldNote: **Money** removes the immediate danger but not the uncertainty; she says so plainly.
Falls back on her father's trade as a hedge, which she would not have considered otherwise.
Hides fear from her mother and shows it to the interviewer, a gap between public and private.

steps.text: Learn domestic wiring with her dad over the summer
Work toward the electrician's licence alongside the degree
Join union meetings weekly and press for a public plan
Write to the local member about retraining pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to argue about it properly. I'd say governments should start now on retraining funds and a shorter working week, and I'd say firms should be required to phase the changes in. I'd put that to the union and to the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the clock more than I show. I'd graduate in about three years and the job market would be half-empty by then. But five years gives me time to build skills that aren't just code, like hardware and safety work, where a person signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree and add a minor in electronics. I'd do a placement in my dad's firm next summer and learn how a real site is run. I'd also finally sit down with an AI assistant, because by then I can't call it hype, and I'd rather learn it while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable but heavy. Like a long exam week with a date I can't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be reacting. With five I can choose. I'd actually use summer placements and ask older students where their jobs went. Time makes me less angry and more practical, which I'm not used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally use an assistant. What changes your mind here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The date. If the end point is certain, then refusing to touch it is just hurting myself. I'd keep my principles about being open when I use it, though, and I'd tell my lecturers every time.

say: I'd call for **retraining funds** and a phased rollout, starting now.
I'd argue in the student paper for a **shorter working week**.
think: I feel the **clock** more than I show.
Five years lets me build skills where a person must **sign off**.
do: Add an **electronics minor** to my computing degree.
Do a **placement** at my dad's firm next summer.
Start using an AI assistant, and **say so** to lecturers.
feel: Heavy but **manageable**, like a long exam week.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be reacting. With five I can choose.
fieldNote: The extra **time** turns her from angry to practical; she names the change herself.
Willing to drop her refusal of AI once the end point is certain, while insisting on honesty.
Still anxious: the job market she graduates into would be thin even with time to prepare.

steps.text: Add an electronics minor to the computing degree
Work a summer placement at her dad's electrical firm
Start using an AI assistant and tell lecturers each time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. I'd say we should use it well: fund retraining, change what schools teach, and not wait for a crisis. I'd also say that a lot can change in a decade, and some predictions will fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly okay. I'd finish my degree, work a few years, and have time to find the parts of engineering where a person has to be there. I'd still be uneasy about whether anyone will hire juniors, but a decade lets me pick a good path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and aim for a master's in embedded systems or robotics. I'd work summers with my dad's firm and save a little from my own wage. I'd also stay in the union, because the rules get written in these ten years and I want a voice in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels quiet. Not calm exactly, more like a held breath that I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you relax about your own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd still not use the tools much, I'd be slower than my classmates, and I'd have to learn that later. But I wouldn't panic. I'd just keep my options wide, which is what my dad says about every business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin picking a degree in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Maya to pick something where people trust a person's signature, like engineering or nursing, and to learn one hands-on skill as well. And to be a bit suspicious of anyone who sounds certain about the date.

say: I'd say use the decade well: fund **retraining** and change what schools teach.
I'd also say some predictions will **fail**, so stay flexible.
think: I'm mostly **okay**, with time to find roles where a person must be there.
I still doubt anyone will hire **juniors**.
do: Finish the degree, then aim for a **master's** in embedded systems or robotics.
Work summers at my dad's firm and save part of the **wage**.
Stay in the **union**, since the rules get written in these years.
feel: Quiet, like a held **breath** I can live with.
S4.quote: I'd tell my cousin Maya to pick something where people trust a person's signature, like engineering or nursing
fieldNote: The long **runway** brings her to a calm plan, but she stays suspicious of confident forecasts.
Uses her father's saying about keeping options wide, a sign of family influence.
Her own AI avoidance remains; she expects to be slower than classmates and accepts that.

steps.text: Apply for a master's in embedded systems or robotics
Save half of each summer wage working at her dad's firm
Stay in the student union and help write its AI policy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because nobody would have time to be fair. What would help is a public plan before it happens: retraining that pays people to study, firms that must explain layoffs, and exams that still prove what a person can do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm lucky and I know it, so I'd like whatever comes to protect people whose parents can't pay. My answers would be harder if my parents couldn't pay.

headlineQuote: I'm lucky and I know it, so I'd like whatever comes to protect people whose parents can't pay.
portrait: Tara is an 18-year-old **computer engineering** student whose family pays everything and who has no debt.
She never uses AI tools, out of pride in her own work and a distrust of the hype.
She is left-leaning and reaches first for the **student union**, rules and public plans, and blames firms rather than students.
Her father's electrical firm gives her a hands-on fallback, which she leans on more as the warning time shrinks.
She moves from calm in the plateau to **anxious** in the fast scenarios, easing as the time lengthens.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because nobody would have time to be fair.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** before it happens: paid retraining, firms explaining layoffs, and exams that prove ability.
